claims: what makes a property of individual executions a safety property in formal terms: every violation is witnessed by a finite prefix of the execution that no continuation can repair, so a violation is irrevocable once it occurs and can in principle be recognized from a finite record of the run, which is what lets a monitor report it, while a run that has not violated the property can in general still go on to violate it

how safety properties are established: by an inductive invariant, a condition that holds in every initial state, is preserved by every step the protocol permits, including steps of faulty processes and losses or delays of messages that the fault model allows, and implies the property, so the argument covers every execution without fairness or eventual progress, and without timing facts unless the protocol relies on a delay bound for safety; and why the invariant that works is often stronger than the property it proves

why many consensus protocols designed for partial synchrony keep safety under any message timing: a decision needs votes from sets of processes large enough that any two overlap in a process that will not vote both ways, as long as faulty processes stay within the threshold, so timing assumptions bear only on progress; and the limit of that independence, since safety is no longer guaranteed when faults that can vote both ways exceed the threshold, and protocols that rely on a delay bound for safety, such as synchronous protocols tolerating more faults or longest-chain protocols, can lose it when the bound is broken

what makes a property of individual executions a liveness property in formal terms: every finite prefix can still be extended to an execution that satisfies it, so no finite observation shows a violation; and why bounded versions, such as a response within a stated time, are safety properties that a finite run can violate

how liveness is argued: a progress measure over a well-founded order, which no step increases and which a step the protocol is assumed eventually to take decreases, and why such arguments need fairness assumptions, such as that a step enabled continuously is eventually taken, without which a scheduler that forever postpones a process's enabled step or a message's delivery can defeat the property when progress depends on that step or message

why, in designs whose safety does not rely on timing, liveness is the part of fault-tolerant agreement that carries timing assumptions: deterministic protocols in a fully asynchronous system in which even one process may crash cannot guarantee termination while keeping agreement and a nontrivial validity condition, so many designs guarantee progress only once delays stay bounded for long enough, or use randomization to terminate with probability one; and what this leaves exposed, since an adversary able to delay messages can postpone decisions for as long as it sustains the delay, without violating safety

the two senses of availability and why they are not interchangeable: the property sense used in partition trade-offs, in which every request reaching a non-failed replica eventually receives a non-error response, and the operational sense, the fraction of a period in which a service answers within a deadline, so a system can meet one and miss the other; and how both differ from data availability, which asks whether published data can be obtained by those who need to check it

for whom a service is available: availability holds only for clients that can reach enough working components, so during a partition a design that needs a quorum or a leader can stay available on the side that has one and unavailable on the other, and an availability claim needs to state which clients it covers

how availability composes along a request path: when a request needs several components in series, its availability is no higher than that of the least available one, and under independent failures it is close to the product of theirs, so a single dependency outside the replicated core, such as a coordinator, gateway or name service, can bound it; and why adding redundant parts raises it only against causes of failure those parts do not share

why availability can be lost while every component is correct: overload, from demand or from denial-of-service attacks, exhausts capacity without requiring any component to fail, so a tolerance bound stated in failed components does not cover it, and admission limits can keep the service available to some requests by refusing others before they consume the capacity that is short

what a consistency model constrains in the replica sense: which values reads may return given the writes, judged against an order of operations, and the questions that separate models, such as whether every observer agrees with one order and whether that order respects real time, with linearizability, sequential, causal and eventual consistency as reference points; and how this sense differs from the transactional one, in which consistency means preserving integrity constraints

why stronger models cost coordination even without failures: keeping one order of operations that every observer agrees with requires, when more than one replica serves operations, some operations to wait for communication with other replicas before they complete, while weaker models such as causal or eventual consistency let a replica answer from its local state, so the choice trades latency against the anomalies clients can observe, such as stale or out-of-order reads

why eventual convergence alone promises little: in its basic form it is a liveness condition that permits any interim values and constrains nothing while updates continue, so weak models add safety constraints clients can rely on, such as causal order or session guarantees like reading one's own writes

how replicas that accept updates independently reconcile concurrent ones: by a rule such as last-writer-wins, which orders every pair of writes without detecting concurrency and can silently discard updates, by detecting concurrency, for example with version vectors, and keeping the conflicting versions, or by merge operations designed to commute, under the delivery the design assumes, so that replicas that have received the same updates converge whatever order they arrived in

masking, fail-safe and non-masking tolerance: which parts of a specification a design keeps while faults within its assumptions are present, whether both its safety and liveness parts, its safety part only by halting or refusing rather than acting wrongly, or an eventual return to correct behavior once faults stop, after a period in which safety may be violated, as in self-stabilizing designs; and why one design can offer different kinds of tolerance against different fault classes

how tolerance differs from fault avoidance and from recovery: avoidance tries to keep faults from arising, tolerance keeps specified properties holding, or for non-masking designs returns to them, while faults are present, within an assumed number and class, by combining redundancy with a rule that masks errors or detects and contains or corrects them, while recovery restores a correct state after a failure has already taken effect; and why a design usually needs recovery as well as tolerance, since tolerance covers only the faults it assumes

what a tolerance claim promises once faults exceed its assumed bound, which correlated failures make more likely than a count of independent faults suggests: nothing by itself, unless the design also establishes, by a separate argument, which property gives way first, such as halting rather than violating safety, or keeping a safety violation attributable to the participants who caused it

statement: Scope: properties of individual executions (trace properties). Properties that compare executions (some forms of confidentiality) are outside; the parent says so, name only, and do not claim confidentiality in general is not safety.

Criterion (Lamport's informal 'nothing bad happens', made formal by Alpern and Schneider): P is safety iff every execution not in P has a finite prefix such that no extension of that prefix is in P. Executions are modeled as infinite; a halted run continues with steps that change nothing.

Irrevocable: once a bad prefix has occurred, every continuation violates P. This is about the execution, not operations: rollback, manual repair or a social-layer fork can restore service but do not un-violate the property for that run.

The 'bad thing' need not be a single state: it can involve a sequence or transition (a decided value later changing; a response with no prior request). Do not write 'only a bad state' (domain prose says 'a state'; history variables reconcile the two, so do not contradict it either).

Monitoring: a monitor that observes every event the property refers to can report a violation at the end of the bad prefix; for a requirement on every state of a run that keeps going, the next step may break it, so while the run continues the monitor can only say 'no violation so far', not that P holds. 'In principle': recognizing a bad prefix can be costly or undecidable for some properties, and a distributed run needs a consistent record of events to judge.
Pitfall: the converse (no finite observation shows a liveness violation; deadline properties are safety) is Liveness's claim. Name the contrast at most; do not explain it.
establishedBy: Inductive invariant I, three obligations: (1) every initial state satisfies I; (2) every step the model permits, taken from ANY state satisfying I (not only reachable states), leads to a state satisfying I; (3) I implies P (for a property over histories, P is checked on states extended with history or auxiliary variables). Induction over steps then covers every execution.

'Every step the model permits' includes steps of processes that follow the protocol, faulty processes' actions as the fault model allows (crash: stop; Byzantine: send any message the model lets it construct), and message loss, delay, reordering or duplication as the model allows. Where faulty processes may behave arbitrarily, their local state is unconstrained, so I speaks of the other processes' state and of messages in transit. A process that only crashes followed the protocol until it stopped, so I constrains its state like any other ('correct' is a property of a whole execution, so under crash faults a state predicate cannot select the correct processes).
No fairness, no 'eventually': this is what separates it from progress arguments (Liveness owns those; name only).

Timing condition: in an untimed (asynchronous) step model the argument never mentions delays. When a protocol relies on a delay bound for safety, the bound is part of the permitted steps and the proof does use it. Do not say safety proofs never involve timing.

Why stronger: P is often not inductive, because some unreachable states satisfy P yet have a permitted step to a violation (for example, a state where a conflicting vote is already in transit). The working invariant adds facts that exclude them, typically about votes cast, values locked and messages in transit. Finding that strengthening is the hard part of the proof.

Testing and monitoring sample executions and can refute, not establish. Model checking and formal specifications are named only (excludes; Model Checking precedent: it owns search and counterexample shapes). 'Invariants' is excluded: the angle here is the proof rule for safety, not invariants as a general design notion.
violatedBy: A reachable step outside what the proof covered: a design flaw (invariant not actually inductive), an implementation that takes steps the model did not include, or a broken assumption.

Faulty processes beyond the threshold, but only of a class that can act inconsistently: equivocation (voting both ways), or crash-recovery that loses persisted votes so a process can vote again differently. Pitfall: in many crash-tolerant protocols (Paxos-style), crashes beyond the threshold halt progress without violating safety. So 'safety can fail / is no longer guaranteed', never 'safety fails' when the threshold is exceeded.

A broken delay bound, for protocols whose safety relies on one: synchronous protocols tolerating more faults; longest-chain protocols, whose fork-resistance analysis assumes bounded delay relative to the block interval as well as an honest majority of mining power or stake.
Longest-chain safety is probabilistic: a confirmed block can be reversed with probability that falls with confirmation depth. Do not present it as a deterministic safety guarantee.
Broken cryptographic assumptions (forged votes) or a membership/threshold configuration in which decision sets no longer overlap (e.g., reconfiguration that does not preserve overlap).
confusions: safety ~ liveness (hazard): split by what each rules out or requires and how each is established; name liveness to draw this boundary only.
Do not restate the parent's decomposition or its finality and halting examples (facet watch). Finality is excluded: no finality example.
Formal 'safety' is not the safety-engineering sense (protection from accidental harm, set against security). One term, one sense.
Formal irrevocability vs operational recovery (see statement).
'No violation observed' vs 'property holds'.

Timing-independent safety is a property of many quorum-based designs, not of all consensus, and not of partial synchrony alone: asynchronous randomized protocols also keep safety under any timing. Do not write 'only' or 'all'.
A system whose agreement core is timing-independent can still rely on timing for safety elsewhere, e.g. lease-based reads that assume bounded clock drift. Do not extend the claim to a whole system.

Quorums, agreement, consensus, fault-models, byzantine-behavior are excluded: state the overlap condition the argument needs, do not explain quorum constructions, sizes, or consensus protocols. Latency excluded.
tradeoffs: Timing-independent safety costs fault tolerance: designs that rely on a delay bound for safety can tolerate more faulty participants (for Byzantine agreement with signatures, a faulty minority rather than fewer than a third) but lose safety when the bound fails. Name the contrast; sizes belong to Quorums.

The overlap argument's condition, stated in full: within one round or view, two decisions need decision sets that share a process that will not vote both ways: under faults that only stop, any shared process (it followed the protocol until it stopped); where some faults can vote both ways, a process outside that faulty set, which holds only while those faults stay within the threshold. A process that follows the protocol votes for at most one value there; across rounds or views it also relies on a rule that processes following the protocol obey (such as carrying votes or locks forward and refusing conflicting proposals), and on those votes persisting (stable storage under crash-recovery). Overlap alone, without that rule, does not give safety. Threshold may be counted in processes or in weight (stake).

statement: Scope: properties of individual executions (trace properties), same scope as Safety. Executions modeled as infinite (a halted run continues with steps that change nothing).

Criterion (Alpern and Schneider): P is liveness iff every finite prefix has at least one extension in P. Consequence: no finite prefix witnesses a violation; a violation is a property of the whole infinite run.

Pitfall on observation: 'no finite observation shows a violation' is the claim. Do not write that observation can never confirm a liveness property: 'eventually p' is confirmed once p occurs; 'p infinitely often' can be neither confirmed nor refuted by a finite record. A stall seen so far is consistent with the property, so it does not by itself show a violation; with knowledge of the protocol a finite record can settle it, e.g. a state from which no permitted continuation reaches the good event.

Bounded versions ('a response within d time units / k steps / r rounds') are safety: the prefix that reaches the bound without the good event witnesses the violation and no continuation repairs it. Condition: the bound is measured in something the execution records (steps, rounds, or real time in a timed model). Name safety for this, do not explain safety's criterion.

Liveness says nothing about how long: a decision after any finite delay satisfies it. What users experience as speed is latency (excluded; name only) and needs bounded, safety-shaped versions plus timing assumptions.

Obligations usually bind processes that keep taking steps (e.g. termination for correct processes); which processes count as correct is the fault model's definition (fault-models excluded: name only). A crashed process is not required to act.
Not every property that is not safety is liveness; that every trace property splits into the two is the parent's statement: do not restate.
establishedBy: Progress measure (ranking function) into a well-founded order (no infinite strictly descending chain: naturals, lexicographic tuples). Obligations, stated over states where the goal has not yet been reached: (1) no permitted step increases the measure (including faulty processes' steps and message delays the model allows); (2) some step, the 'helpful' one, decreases it or reaches the goal; (3) fairness ensures the helpful step is eventually taken. Since the measure cannot decrease forever, the goal is reached.

Fairness conditions: weak fairness = a step continuously enabled is eventually taken; strong fairness = a step enabled infinitely often is eventually taken. Pair the rule with the fairness kind it uses; the helpful step must stay enabled (weak) or recur (strong) until taken. Fairness on channels: every message sent between correct processes is eventually delivered.

Why fairness is needed: without it, a permitted execution can postpone the helpful step forever (never schedule a waiting process's step, never deliver a message), and the measure never decreases. Fairness is an assumption about the scheduler or environment, not something the protocol enforces; it is itself liveness-shaped, so no finite run can show it was violated.

Partial synchrony: the helpful step is often available only once delays are bounded (e.g. a correct leader's messages arriving before timeouts), so the argument holds only after stabilization. Variants (Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer): a delay bound exists but is unknown, or a known bound holds only after an unknown stabilization time. Processes do not know when stabilization occurs.

Randomized protocols: the measure decreases with some probability per round (bounded away from zero, given the adversary's limits); the conclusion is termination with probability one, not in every run.
Contrast with safety's invariant rule: name only to draw the boundary (safety ~ liveness hazard). Formal specifications and temporal-logic proof systems are excluded: name at most.
violatedBy: An infinite run in which the good event never occurs. Forms: livelock (steps keep happening but the measure never decreases, e.g. competing proposers repeatedly preempting each other); starvation (some process's request never served while others progress); indefinite postponement by message delay; faults beyond the threshold that halt progress (the parent's halting example: name, do not restate).
Pitfall: 'no deadlock' stated as 'never reach a state with no enabled step' is a safety property (a bad state). Do not use deadlock as the archetype of a liveness violation without that care.

A broken fairness or timing assumption: an unfair scheduler, unbounded delay, stabilization that never comes. For randomized designs, an adversary that can predict or bias coin outcomes, beyond what the design tolerates.

Exposure (claim 3), scoped: in designs whose safety does not rely on timing and whose progress needs bounded delay, an adversary controlling delay (keeping messages beyond the protocol's timeouts, or targeting each successive leader) can postpone decisions for as long as it sustains it, with faults within the threshold and safety intact. In designs that rely on a delay bound for safety, the same delay can break safety (Safety's territory: name only). Against classic randomized asynchronous designs, delay slows decisions in real time but does not make non-termination more than a probability-zero event, as long as the adversary cannot predict the coins.

Detection pitfall: a sustained postponement is indistinguishable in finite time from slow progress; operators see a missed bound (a safety-shaped surrogate), not a proven liveness violation. Fault detection is excluded: name only.
confusions: safety ~ liveness (hazard): split by what each rules out or requires and how each is established (extension criterion and progress measure under fairness here; finite bad prefix and inductive invariant there). Name safety to draw the boundary; do not explain its criterion, invariant rule or quorum-overlap argument.

availability ~ liveness (hazard): liveness is the eventual-progress shape any property can take; availability protects the service and its data, and its partition sense is one liveness-shaped property. Do not discuss service availability, uptime or clients covered. Keep 'availability is not liveness' true.
Censorship resistance is named at most (a liveness-shaped commitment about each valid action); do not explain it.
Liveness vs latency: eventual vs bounded; a guarantee with no bound gives no response time.
'Fairness' here is scheduling fairness (enabled steps are eventually taken), not fair transaction ordering or economic fairness. One term, one sense.
Probability one is not certainty: non-terminating runs exist but have probability zero.

FLP is about guaranteeing termination in every admissible run of a deterministic protocol; it does not say consensus never terminates in practice, nor that agreement or validity must fail. Consensus and agreement are excluded: state the result's conditions, do not explain consensus protocols or the agreement property.
Do not restate the parent's decomposition, its 'never finalizing anything' example or the halting example (facet watch). Finality excluded: no finality example.
relation: FLP (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson 1985), all conditions: deterministic processes; fully asynchronous (no bound on message delay or on relative process speeds, no synchronized clocks); reliable channels (every message eventually delivered, so loss is not the cause); at most one process may fail, by crashing (crash-stop); required: agreement, nontrivial validity (each of two values is decided in some run), and termination in every admissible run. Conclusion: no protocol guarantees all three; some admissible run never decides. That run need contain no crash: the possibility of one suffices.

Ways designs proceed despite FLP, not exhaustive: guarantee progress only once delays stay bounded long enough (partial synchrony; safety kept under any timing in many quorum-based designs); randomization, terminating with probability one (e.g. Ben-Or style, under thresholds and with coins the adversary cannot predict; expected rounds depend on the coin design); failure detectors, which encapsulate timing assumptions (fault-detection excluded: name only); synchrony assumptions, as in longest-chain protocols, which also weaken agreement to a probabilistic form. Do not write 'the only' or 'the two ways'.

Pitfall: 'make progress only during periods of bounded delay' is wrong as worded; deterministic designs can decide during asynchronous periods, they are only not guaranteed to. Use 'guaranteed only once'.

Pitfall: 'liveness is the part that carries timing assumptions' holds for designs whose safety does not rely on timing; synchronous and longest-chain protocols rely on a delay bound for safety too (Safety's claim). Scope it: 'in many designs' / 'in designs whose safety is timing-independent'.
tradeoffs: Under asynchrony with possible crashes (FLP conditions), a deterministic design cannot guarantee both safety and termination; designs built for partial synchrony keep safety unconditionally and make liveness conditional on timing, choosing to stall rather than decide inconsistently.

Timeouts: short timeouts recover sooner from a faulty leader but can fire spuriously during slow periods and keep a protocol from deciding; many designs grow timeouts so that, once delays are bounded, they eventually exceed the delay. Name only; latency excluded.

model.meaning: The property that a service, and the data it serves, can be obtained by the clients that request it; one word with two senses (eventual non-error response from every non-failed replica; measured fraction of a period answered within a deadline), so the sentence must cover both without picking one.

parents.protocol-properties: Parent names availability as protecting 'the service and its data' and uses it in the partition trade-off (keep answering on every side vs one up-to-date order). Adds: that the trade-off uses the partition sense, which differs from measured uptime; for which clients a claim holds; how it composes along a request path; loss through overload with no failed component. Do not restate the partition sentence or the 'defined by what they protect' sentence; no 'pick two' wording.
parents.security-properties: Parent says availability concerns the service as a whole, is judged 'by how much of the time the system works' (the measured sense), and that ledgers buy it by replicating everything. Adds: a measured fraction hides which clients were excluded; replication raises availability of the replicated core, while the request path can still be bounded by a single dependency outside it and by shared causes of failure; overload, including denial-of-service, removes it without any component failing. Must not contradict the parent's replication sentence: qualify it (scope), do not deny it. Do not restate the availability vs censorship-resistance sentence.

claims: the two senses of availability and why they are not interchangeable: the property sense used in partition trade-offs, in which every request reaching a non-failed replica eventually receives a non-error response, and the operational sense, the fraction of a period in which a service answers within a deadline, so a system can meet one and miss the other; and how both differ from data availability, which asks whether published data can be obtained by those who need to check it

for whom a service is available: availability holds only for clients that can reach enough working components, so during a partition a design that needs a quorum or a leader can stay available on the side that has one and unavailable on the other, and an availability claim needs to state which clients it covers

how availability composes along a request path: when a request needs several components in series, its availability is no higher than that of the least available one, and under independent failures it is close to the product of theirs, so a single dependency outside the replicated core, such as a coordinator, gateway or name service, can bound it; and why adding redundant parts raises it only against causes of failure those parts do not share

why availability can be lost while every component is correct: overload, from demand or from denial-of-service attacks, exhausts capacity without requiring any component to fail, so a tolerance bound stated in failed components does not cover it, and admission limits can keep the service available to some requests by refusing others before they consume the capacity that is short

placements.availability: Leaf under Protocol Properties beside safety, liveness, consistency, fault-tolerance, finality, censorship-resistance. Parent uses the partition sense; the record states that sense with its model (non-failing replicas, unbounded response time, network that may lose messages) and also the measured sense, so it stands without the parent. Consistency, liveness and fault tolerance are siblings: named only. No positional or 'in this domain' wording.
placements.availability-in-security-properties: Leaf under Security Properties beside safety, liveness, integrity, confidentiality, censorship-resistance. Parent uses the measured sense; same one exposition holds because both senses are defined in the record, and the adversary enters as overload (denial-of-service, named only) or as an induced partition, both stated as conditions, not as a security-only framing. Must keep true the domain sentences 'Availability is not liveness', 'censorship resistance is not generic availability' and 'Redundancy does not guarantee availability'.

statement: Subject: the service as a whole and the data it serves to its clients (parent: 'the service and its data'). Not the publication of committed data for verification (that is Data Availability: name only) and not each valid action (Censorship Resistance: name only).

Partition sense (Gilbert and Lynch's formalization of Brewer's conjecture): every request received by a non-failed replica eventually gets a response; the plan's 'non-error' is the usual reading of that response. Conditions to keep: 'non-failed' is defined by the fault model (crash/omission in that formalization; do not carry it to Byzantine replicas without saying so); no time bound ('eventually'); the response need not reflect the latest writes (that is consistency's concern, named only). It says nothing about requests that reach no non-failed replica.

Measured (operational) sense: the fraction of a stated period in which the service answers within a stated deadline, measured from some vantage point; also often computed over requests (successful requests / all requests) rather than time. The number depends on the deadline, the success criterion, the vantage point and the request mix chosen; state that, do not present one number as intrinsic.

Meet one, miss the other (both directions, with conditions): (a) a majority-quorum design can show a high measured fraction yet fail the partition sense, because replicas cut off from a majority refuse or stall during a partition for operations that need the quorum (the high fraction holds when partitions are rare or short); (b) a design can satisfy the partition sense yet score poorly on the measured sense, since the partition sense sets no deadline and imposes nothing on requests that reach no non-failed replica (e.g. while replicas are down), whereas the measured sense counts slow answers and downtime as failures.

Shape: the partition sense has two parts: its eventual-response part is liveness-shaped (no deadline), and its non-error part constrains what the answer may be, not when it comes. Do not classify the non-error part as safety: the requirement binds only replicas that do not fail, so where the fault model lets a replica stop later, an error answer is not a violation that no continuation repairs. Name the liveness shape only; do not explain liveness or safety, and do not call the whole requirement liveness. The measured sense is a statistic over a period, not a property every execution must satisfy; do not call it a liveness or safety property. Do not say availability is liveness (domain prose: 'Availability is not liveness').

Scope of coverage: an availability statement names which clients (and, where designs differ, which operations, e.g. reads vs writes) it covers; a high aggregate can coexist with some clients fully cut off. Quorum/leader pitfall: keep 'can stay available'. A leader-based design that also needs a quorum to commit is not available on the leader's side if that side lacks a majority (the leader cannot commit; the majority side may be unavailable until it elects a new leader); if no side holds a quorum, no side is available for those operations. Do not write 'the side with the leader stays available' unconditionally.
establishedBy: Partition sense: by design argument over the model, i.e. the operation can complete from what a replica can reach; a replica that must hear from others before answering cannot guarantee a response when messages can be lost indefinitely, as that model allows. Name only that this is where the consistency trade-off bites; do not explain consistency models or restate the parent's partition sentence.

Measured sense: by measurement over a past period (probes, request logs, service-level objectives) and by estimate from component figures (composition, see relation). Measurement samples behavior; it is not a guarantee over all executions (parent's property vs observed behavior distinction: do not restate it, but do not present a measured figure as a proven property either).
Estimates depend on assumed failure and repair rates and on independence; state the assumption when giving a figure.
violatedBy: Partition sense: a non-failed replica that returns an error or never responds, e.g. one that refuses because it cannot reach a quorum or leader.

Measured sense: time or requests beyond the stated budget: components down beyond what redundancy covers; clients partitioned from enough working components; a failure in a series dependency; a common-cause failure across redundant parts; overload pushing answers past the deadline or into refusal.

Overload while every component is correct: capacity exhausted by demand or by denial-of-service attacks (named only). Condition: where the fault model counts a component that follows its protocol as correct however slowly it runs, nothing has failed, so a tolerance bound stated as 'up to f failed components' (fault tolerance, named only) does not cover it; where late responses count as timing failures, overload that slows many components at once can exceed such a bound instead. Pitfalls: overload can also produce real failures (out-of-memory crashes), which do count against the bound; and it can feed on itself (timeouts make failure detection wrongly suspect slow but correct nodes, triggering failover or retries that add load), but a correct node wrongly suspected is not a failure and does not count against the bound. Do not write that overload never causes failures; and not every denial-of-service is overload (some exploit crash bugs, which are failures).
confusions: availability ~ liveness (hazard): liveness is the eventual-progress shape any property can take; availability is defined by what it protects. Only the partition sense has liveness shape; the measured sense has a deadline and is a statistic. Name liveness, explain nothing of its criterion, proof or fairness.

availability ~ censorship resistance: service as a whole vs each valid action; parent already makes this contrast, so do not restate it. At most one naming sentence if needed for the coverage claim (refusing particular clients' requests on purpose is censorship resistance's subject, not explained here).

availability ~ data availability (authored concept): data availability asks whether data a system has committed to can be obtained in full by those who need to verify it, in time. Different subject (published data, verifiers, withholding) and different adversary; a service can answer its clients while data needed for verification is withheld. Name with its key property only; do not explain sampling, committees or the withholding argument.
partition sense ~ measured uptime: the facet-watch distinction; keep the two labeled distinctly throughout (one term, one sense per sentence). The parent of each placement uses a different one.
available ~ correct or up to date: a non-error response is not a correct or current one; consistency and integrity are separate properties (name only).

redundancy ~ availability: redundancy (named only) raises availability only against failures the redundant parts do not share and only for components it replicates; domain prose 'Redundancy does not guarantee availability' must stay true.
Do not write 'pick two of three' or restate the CAP trade-off; the parent states it.
relation: Series (a request needs every component): availability of the path is at most the minimum of the components' availabilities. This bound needs no independence: the path is up only when each component is up. Condition: availabilities measured in the same sense, over the same period and requests; caching, fallbacks or retries can take a component out of strict series.

Under independent failures the path's availability is (close to) the product: e.g. five components at 99.9% give about 99.5% (0.999^5 = 0.99501). Without independence the product is not the answer: positively correlated failures (that tend to coincide) put it between the product and the minimum; the minimum bound always holds. Never state the product without its independence condition.
Consequence: one dependency outside the replicated core (coordinator, gateway, name service, a single access endpoint to a replicated network) bounds the path however well the core is replicated.

Parallel (any one of k parts suffices): under independence unavailability multiplies, 1 - product of (1 - A_i); a shared cause of failure (same software defect, same configuration push, same power, region or provider) acts like a single component in series with the redundant set, so the set is no more available than that cause allows. Redundancy still helps against causes the parts do not share; do not write that any shared cause makes redundancy useless. Failover detection and switching time counts as downtime for requests arriving during it, and failover machinery can itself be a series component.
Keep arithmetic illustrative and correct; do not attach invented figures to real systems.
tradeoffs: Admission limits (rate limiting and denial-of-service resistance named only; load shedding, quotas; if fees are used as an example, keep it to general admission, not exclusion of particular parties, which is censorship resistance's subject) can keep the service available to some requests by refusing others before they consume the capacity that is short; a limit that refuses only after that capacity is spent (e.g. a flood saturating the link in front of a server's rate limiter) does not protect the requests it admits. The refused requests are unavailable to their clients, so this chooses whom availability covers rather than raising it for everyone. A refusal is an error response: it does not satisfy the partition sense for that request.
Availability vs consistency during a partition: parent's trade-off; name only.
Coverage vs aggregate: designs and measurements can trade a few clients' total loss for a high average; why the coverage statement is part of the claim.

design.relationship: One word, two senses that the two parents each use (partition sense under Protocol Properties, measured fraction under Security Properties), plus a third concept sharing the word (data availability): a real conflation, followed by conditions (coverage, composition arithmetic with its independence condition, overload) that are arguments best carried in prose.

Liveness, consistency and fault tolerance own the shape, the replica-order models and tolerance bounds respectively, so none of them should carry these claims.

model.meaning: Note: replica sense only (domain prose: what different participants may observe of the same state). A consistency model is a constraint on which values reads may return given the writes, stated against an order of operations (or, for eventual consistency, only as convergence).

parents.protocol-properties: Parent names consistency as protecting the relation between what participants observe, and states the partition trade-off (keep some availability or some consistency). Adds: what a model constrains and what separates the reference models; the failure-free coordination cost; why bare convergence is weak and what weak models add; how independently accepted concurrent updates are detected and resolved. Do not restate the parent's partition sentence or its safety/liveness decomposition; name them at most.

claims: what a consistency model constrains in the replica sense: which values reads may return given the writes, judged against an order of operations, and the questions that separate models, such as whether every observer agrees with one order and whether that order respects real time, with linearizability, sequential, causal and eventual consistency as reference points; and how this sense differs from the transactional one, in which consistency means preserving integrity constraints

why stronger models cost coordination even without failures: keeping one order of operations that every observer agrees with requires, when more than one replica serves operations, some operations to wait for communication with other replicas before they complete, while weaker models such as causal or eventual consistency let a replica answer from its local state, so the choice trades latency against the anomalies clients can observe, such as stale or out-of-order reads

why eventual convergence alone promises little: in its basic form it is a liveness condition that permits any interim values and constrains nothing while updates continue, so weak models add safety constraints clients can rely on, such as causal order or session guarantees like reading one's own writes

how replicas that accept updates independently reconcile concurrent ones: by a rule such as last-writer-wins, which orders every pair of writes without detecting concurrency and can silently discard updates, by detecting concurrency, for example with version vectors, and keeping the conflicting versions, or by merge operations designed to commute, under the delivery the design assumes, so that replicas that have received the same updates converge whatever order they arrived in

placements.consistency: Single placement, under Protocol Properties in Foundations; general replicated-data framing, no ledger-specific sense needed. The record must still stand alone (L2), so state the replica sense in its own words rather than leaning on the parent's phrase.

statement: A model is a set of allowed histories: given the writes (and their timing/issuing client), which values each read may return. Judged against an order of operations the history must be explainable by.

Separating questions the claim names: is there one order every observer agrees with; does that order respect real time (an operation completed before another started comes first). Add only what the claims need; no full hierarchy, no isolation levels, no per-object composability.

Reference points: linearizability (one order, respects real time: each operation takes effect at some point between its invocation and its response); sequential (one order, respects each client's own order, not real time across clients); causal (observers agree on the order of causally related operations only; concurrent writes may be seen in different orders by different observers); eventual (basic form: if updates stop, replicas eventually return the same value; says nothing about interim reads).

Transactional sense (ACID C): a transaction preserves the application's integrity constraints. Different question: which states are valid, not what different observers see. Name Transactions only; do not explain atomicity or isolation.
establishedBy: Strong models (linearizable, sequential): some operations wait for communication with other replicas before completing. Condition: holds when more than one replica serves operations; a design with a single node answering everything pays instead in clients' round trips to it and, unless it replicates a write before answering, in losing that write if it fails. Which operations wait (reads, writes, or both) is a design choice; the basic lower bound (in a model with a known minimum message delay) applies to a read and a write together, so a design can make one fast at the other's expense; do not state a per-operation bound.

Coordination here means waiting for messages (e.g. quorum round trips), not necessarily consensus: linearizable read/write registers can be built without solving consensus (crash faults, a majority correct, asynchronous); general operations such as compare-and-swap, or a replicated state machine, do need agreement. Do not write 'strong consistency requires consensus'. Agreement is named only.

How replicas apply one sequence and where a read is placed in it (read ordered as an input, read after the last fixed position, leader-local reads under timing assumptions) belongs to State Machine Replication: name, do not explain.

Weak models: a replica answers reads and accepts writes from local state and propagates later. Causal: a replica makes a remote write visible only once the writes it depends on are visible there (tracking dependencies costs metadata, not waits on other replicas at answer time). Session guarantees: per client session; serving them locally needs the client to stay with replicas that have its session's writes, or to carry what it has seen so a replica that lacks them waits or refuses.

Convergence by reconciliation (claim 4): not every rule detects concurrency. Last-writer-wins orders every pair of writes by timestamp without detecting concurrency. Keeping concurrent versions for the application to resolve needs concurrency detected, e.g. with version vectors (one dominates -> ordered; neither -> concurrent); physical timestamps (any single number) cannot detect it. Merges designed to commute combine updates, many without detecting concurrency; under their delivery assumptions they guarantee convergence, not that every concurrent update survives: how much each keeps depends on the type (grow-only counters and sets keep everything; last-writer-wins registers, max registers, add-wins and remove-wins sets drop effects).
violatedBy: Anomalies a model may forbid or permit: stale reads; out-of-order reads (an effect seen before its cause); successive reads by one client going backwards as it moves between replicas; a client not seeing its own write. Which is a violation depends on the model: sequential consistency can still permit reads stale in real time; causal permits stale reads.

Last-writer-wins silently discards all concurrent writes except the winner. With physical clock timestamps and clock skew it can also discard a write that causally followed the winner; timestamps that respect causality (logical/hybrid clocks) avoid that case but still drop concurrent writes. Deterministic, so replicas converge; the loss is the cost.

Merges converge only under their delivery assumptions: state-based merges must also be associative and idempotent (duplicates, any order); operation-based designs commonly need exactly-once and causal delivery, with only concurrent operations required to commute. 'Whatever the delivery order' holds within those assumptions, not unconditionally.

Convergence is not invariant preservation: two updates each valid alone can merge into a state violating an application constraint (e.g. a balance below zero, a duplicate unique name); keeping such constraints needs coordination. Keep to one sentence; do not drift into transactions.
confusions: Replica consistency vs ACID consistency (facet watch): same word, different question.

Eventual consistency is not just the weakest point on the strength scale: in basic form it is a liveness condition (Liveness, Safety named only), constraining nothing while updates continue; weak models add safety constraints (causal order, session guarantees) on top.
Causal consistency alone does not require replicas to converge on concurrent writes; convergence is a separate addition (causal plus convergence). Do not write that causal implies eventual.
A stale answer is not by itself a fault: whether it is acceptable is what the model says (SMR's record already points here).
Consistency vs Finality: a completed write under a model is not finality; name Finality only. Consistency vs availability under partition: parent's sentence; name only, do not restate.
'Strong consistency' is ambiguous (often linearizability, sometimes sequential or strict serializability); avoid or define.
variants: Reference points by strength as histories allowed: every linearizable history is sequentially consistent, every sequentially consistent one is causally consistent; eventual is a different kind of constraint (convergence), not the next point on the chain. Strength only as far as the claims need.
Session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, and similar) are per-client constraints that can be added to a weak model; name one or two, do not catalog.
tradeoffs: Failure-free cost: latency of waiting operations vs anomalies clients can observe (stale, out-of-order reads). Latency named only.
Under partitions the trade-off is availability vs consistency: parent owns that sentence; at most a back-reference, no restatement.

Accepting writes at any replica independently buys local answers for writes as well as reads, and pays with reconciliation: lost updates (last-writer-wins), merge-restricted data types, or application-level resolution of kept conflicting versions.

design.relationship: A family of models told apart by the same questions (one agreed order? tied to real time? can a replica answer locally?), plus a term the reader conflates with a different sense of the same word. The coordination cost, the weakness of bare convergence and the reconciliation of concurrent updates are causal arguments with conditions.

model.meaning: A design's guarantee that its specified properties keep holding (all of them, or only the safety part) or are returned to once faults stop, while faults stay within an assumed class and number; outside those assumptions it promises nothing unless a separate argument covers those executions.

parents.protocol-properties: Parent already says: FT is a claim about other properties (which survive, through which faults, how many); incomplete until it names survivors; they survive differently; consensus halting rather than finalizing conflicting results. Do not restate any of it, nor reuse the halting example as the main illustration. Adds: the named kinds (masking, fail-safe, non-masking) as the vocabulary for 'survive differently'; one design, different kinds per fault class; tolerance vs avoidance vs recovery; what the claim promises past its bound.
parents.distributed-storage: Parent already says: storage FT = how many correlated losses a design absorbs; independence of copies beats count; repair restores a decaying margin. Do not restate correlation-vs-copies or explain repair. Adds: the general bounded-guarantee frame the storage sentence applies; correlation changes the likelihood of exceeding the bound, not the bound; what a storage design can promise past its bound (e.g., failing reads rather than returning wrong data, see violatedBy/variants notes).
parents.resilience: Parent covers graceful degradation, efficiency vs resilience, correlated failures, recovery as coordination; the domain distinction 'Fault Tolerance ≠ Resilience ≠ Recovery ≠ Account Recovery' already exists. Adds: FT as the 'continued operation within assumed faults' part, its kinds, and its boundary with avoidance and recovery, without explaining resilience, recovery, graceful degradation or failure isolation.
parents.self-healing: Parent covers detecting faults and responding on its own (failover, reduced form, restoring state). Domain prose: 'fault tolerance does not eliminate faults'. Adds: tolerance as a property fixed by design for assumed faults, vs responses after a fault; non-masking (self-stabilizing) tolerance as a guaranteed return, without equating self-healing with it and without explaining failover, recovery modes or state repair.

claims: masking, fail-safe and non-masking tolerance: which parts of a specification a design keeps while faults within its assumptions are present, whether both its safety and liveness parts, its safety part only by halting or refusing rather than acting wrongly, or an eventual return to correct behavior once faults stop, after a period in which safety may be violated, as in self-stabilizing designs; and why one design can offer different kinds of tolerance against different fault classes

how tolerance differs from fault avoidance and from recovery: avoidance tries to keep faults from arising, tolerance keeps specified properties holding, or for non-masking designs returns to them, while faults are present, within an assumed number and class, by combining redundancy with a rule that masks errors or detects and contains or corrects them, while recovery restores a correct state after a failure has already taken effect; and why a design usually needs recovery as well as tolerance, since tolerance covers only the faults it assumes

what a tolerance claim promises once faults exceed its assumed bound, which correlated failures make more likely than a count of independent faults suggests: nothing by itself, unless the design also establishes, by a separate argument, which property gives way first, such as halting rather than violating safety, or keeping a safety violation attributable to the participants who caused it

placements.fault-tolerance: Leaf under Protocol Properties beside Safety and Liveness: the kinds are stated in terms of a specification's safety and liveness parts, which those siblings own; reference the parts by name, never their formal definitions, proofs, quorum-intersection or timing arguments.
placements.fault-tolerance-in-distributed-storage: Holds for storage: a storage design's specification (data retrievable, reads return what was written) has the same safety/liveness parts and the same bounded, assumption-relative guarantee. Pick at least one example or phrasing that is not consensus-specific so the text does not read as consensus-only; no storage-only claim.
placements.fault-tolerance-in-resilience: Holds as the continued-operation facet named in the Resilience parent; text must not define resilience or depend on that parent. No security-only claim; adversarial faults enter only as a fault class (Fault Models owns classes).
placements.fault-tolerance-in-self-healing: Holds where protocols respond automatically: tolerance is what the design guarantees within its assumptions, detection-and-response mechanisms are one way it is built (named only). No claim that all self-healing is fault tolerance or vice versa.

statement: A conditioned claim: specified properties (named), against a fault class and bound (from the fault model, named only), under a timing model where it matters.

Three kinds by what of the specification is kept while assumed faults occur: masking = safety and liveness parts both hold; fail-safe = safety part holds, liveness may be lost (stops/refuses rather than acting wrongly); non-masking = safety may be violated for a while, but the system returns to correct behavior once faults stop (or stay absent long enough to converge). Self-stabilizing designs are the extreme non-masking case: from any state, for transient faults that corrupt state, with the code itself intact.
Condition pitfall: the non-masking return is promised only after faults cease; do not write it as holding 'while faults are present'.

Keep 'safety'/'liveness' in the specification sense the siblings own; masking guarantees are usually stated for correct processes where the fault class allows faulty ones to deviate (do not say 'stated over correct processes' as a universal; uniform variants exist under crash/omission, owned by Fault Models).
establishedBy: Redundancy in some form (extra replicas, repeated attempts in time, redundant information such as codes/checksums) plus a rule that uses it: masking typically via rules that outvote or outnumber faulty contributions (voting, quorum-style rules) or via error-correcting information; detection plus containment (stop, refuse, exclude) for fail-safe; detection plus correction for non-masking. Redundancy is named only; do not explain replication, quorums or voting thresholds.

Argued, not observed: the claim covers every execution within the assumptions (parent Protocol Properties already says properties are established by reasoning; do not restate). Safety/liveness proof techniques belong to siblings.

Pitfall: the redundancy-managing element (voter, coordinator, detector) is itself a component; if it is not covered by the assumptions it can become the single point whose fault defeats the claim. Say 'can', not 'is'.
violatedBy: Within the assumptions: a flaw in the design or implementation of the masking/detection rule (the claim was simply false).

Outside the assumptions the claim is not violated but void: more faults than the bound, or faults outside the class (e.g., a crash-recovery process that loses state it had acted on, under a model that did not allow it — Fault Models owns why). Correlated causes (shared software, operator, host, region, key) make exceeding the bound likelier than an independent-fault count suggests; a common-mode design fault in identical replicas can strike all of them at once, so adding identical replicas does not tolerate it. Correlation does not change the bound; it changes how likely executions beyond it are.

Overlap watch: Availability owns 'redundant parts raise availability only against causes they do not share' and parents state correlation; FT's angle is only the likelihood of leaving the assumed bound and what the claim then promises.
confusions: Tolerance vs avoidance: avoidance (prevention and removal of faults, e.g., careful engineering, verification, testing) reduces faults arising; tolerance assumes they will arise within a bound. 'Fault tolerance does not eliminate faults' (domain prose).

Tolerance vs recovery (Recovery named only): one term, one sense — reserve 'recovery' for restoring a correct state after a failure has taken effect, typically beyond or outside the design's tolerance claim (restart, restore, coordinated intervention). The non-masking return is the hard case: it also follows a period of violation, but it is a guaranteed part of the design's own behavior for its assumed faults; draw that line explicitly so the record does not contradict itself. Within-design error correction should not be called 'recovery' in the record (dependability literature does; avoid the second sense).

Why both are needed: tolerance covers only assumed faults; faults outside the class or beyond the bound leave recovery (and avoidance) as what remains. Say 'usually'; not every system has a recovery path.

Fail-safe tolerance vs the engineering 'fail-safe state' and vs graceful degradation: fail-safe here is relative to the specification's safety part; halting is 'safe' only if the safety part does not itself require timely action. Where the environment keeps moving while the system is halted (prices, external deadlines), keeping a safety property can require acting, e.g., a collateral invariant that holds only if under-collateralized positions are liquidated in time, so halting need not preserve it. (That bounded deadlines are safety properties is the Liveness sibling's point; reference only.) Graceful degradation (reduced function) is named only.
Fault tolerance vs resilience: named only; domain-level distinction exists, do not redraw it.
variants: One design, different kinds per fault class (claim 1 second half). Simplest safe example: a design can mask crashes of up to its bound of replicas while being only non-masking (self-stabilizing) against transient corruption of state. A timing example (consensus keeping safety but missing a decision deadline when delays exceed a bound) is fail-safe only relative to a specification with that deadline, where late messages count as performance faults, and only for designs whose safety does not rely on timing (Safety/Liveness siblings own why); under plain partial synchrony, periods of long delay are inside the model, not faults. Use it only with those conditions stated, or avoid it. Use 'many'/'can', never 'every'.

Past the bound (claim 3): by itself the claim promises nothing; a design can additionally establish (by a separate argument, not merely state) which property gives way first. Which one gives way can depend on which class exceeds the bound: too many silent/crashed participants can leave a quorum-based protocol halted with safety intact, while too many participants that vote both ways can break safety (Safety sibling owns the threshold argument; name only). Attributable violation (accountable safety), in designs built for it: if safety breaks, signed protocol messages can identify participants that provably broke the protocol (some designs guarantee a stated minimum share of them); needs signatures and access to the conflicting messages; it does not prevent or undo the violation; consequences belong to Accountability (named only).

Storage-fitting past-bound example, if used: a reader that checks data against a hash it already trusts gets an error rather than wrong data once too many copies are lost or corrupted (fail-safe beyond bound for integrity; retrievability lost). Condition: the reader verifies against a trusted digest.
tradeoffs: Masking often costs more redundancy and coordination than fail-safe for the same faults (not in every design); fail-safe trades liveness for safety; non-masking accepts temporary safety violations for a guaranteed return (and often cheaper or more general coverage of transient faults). Keep it qualitative; resource numbers belong to Fault Models.
Do not let this become a sibling's or Redundancy's cost argument; one sentence at most.

design.relationship: A conditioned guarantee and its qualifications: kinds of tolerance defined by which parts of a specification survive under which conditions, a boundary with avoidance and recovery that turns on when and by whom correctness is kept or restored, and what the claim promises outside its assumptions. The meaning is argument, condition and qualification.
design.whyProse: The three kinds differ on two short facts each (safety kept, liveness kept or return after faults stop), stated in one sentence; a comparison table would show a trivial truth table and drop the conditions that make it true (return only once faults stop, fail-safe relative to the safety part, per-fault-class kinds). Tolerance vs avoidance vs recovery is already drawn as a domain-level distinction (Fault Tolerance ≠ Resilience ≠ Recovery) and the hard case (non-masking return vs recovery) needs an argued condition, not an A ≠ B. The past-bound claim is conditional reasoning (which property gives way, under which class, with what evidence). No order, loop, persistent states or tension pair carries meaning here.
design.level: These claims are about the tolerance claim itself (its kinds, its boundary with neighboring approaches, its behavior past the bound); the parents only state that FT names surviving properties or absorbs correlated losses, and Fault Models owns classes and thresholds, so the analysis belongs at this concept.
design.territory: Draws no sibling relationship: safety/liveness are referenced as parts of a specification, not defined or proven; Availability's composition and shared-cause redundancy point is not repeated; Fault Models' classes, nesting and thresholds, and Redundancy, Graceful Degradation, Failure Isolation, Recovery, Automatic Failover, Fault Detection, Accountability and Resilience are named only.

audit.note: First audit (auditor A), complete, of the freshly drafted record (prose, four paragraphs, 896 words, as designed). Overlap per placement: Protocol Properties: no parent sentence restated; the definition adds the three kinds to the parent's 'which properties survive', and the parent's halting example appears only as the stalled half of a class-dependent contrast that makes a new point. Distributed Storage: the parent's correlated-losses and independence-over-count point is not restated; the record adds that correlation changes how likely executions beyond the bound are, not the bound, and the storage examples (erasure-coded store masking fragment loss, trusted-digest reader) keep the text from reading as consensus-only. Resilience: the parent's graceful-degradation priorities, efficiency-versus-resilience and recovery-as-coordination are not restated, and the domain distinction is not redrawn. Self-Healing: the parent's detect-and-respond framing is not restated; detection and failover are tolerance only where the design argues their outcome, and no equation of self-healing with tolerance is made. Territory: Fault Models, Redundancy, Graceful Degradation, Recovery, Automatic Failover, Fault Detection, Safety, Liveness and Accountability are named only; Failure Isolation, Resilience, Disaster Recovery, Byzantine Behavior and Data Replication are not named or explained; recovery gets the one contrast sentence the claim requires and nothing of its mechanism. Safety's threshold argument is deferred ('for reasons that belong to Safety'); Availability's composition and shared-cause argument is not repeated. All three claims are explained. Accuracy: masking, fail-safe and non-masking match the Arora-Kulkarni sense (safety and liveness kept; safety kept by halting or refusing; temporary violation with return once faults stop for long enough); self-stabilization is stated with its transient-fault scope, intact code and assumed scheduling. Fail-safe is relative to the safety part: halting trivially preserves a property that only forbids the system's own actions but not an environment-dependent invariant, and the lending example illustrates that correctly. Flagged items: 'masking often needs more redundancy and coordination than fail-safe' is hedged and supported (masking combines detection with correction, fail-safe needs detection only; duplex comparison versus triple voting, detecting versus correcting codes); the replicated service that masks crashes but offers only non-masking tolerance against transient state corruption is an existence claim ('can') supported by self-stabilizing replicated state machine designs, and it correctly illustrates per-fault-class kinds. Avoidance (prevention and removal) versus tolerance versus recovery is drawn without contradiction, including the non-masking hard case (a guaranteed return by the design's own rules for assumed faults). Past the bound: excess or out-of-class faults void rather than falsify the claim, a flaw in the rule falsifies it; the vote-set contrast is scoped to 'many protocols that decide by overlapping vote sets'; the trusted-digest reader carries its collision-resistance condition; accountable safety carries obtainable messages and unforgeable signatures, identifies 'at least some' violators and neither prevents nor undoes the violation. Every absolute checked. Canonical validity: no positional or dated words; holds at all four placements; American English. Structure: prose as designed; no order, loop, state or real conflation is buried. Depth fits the three claims. Advisory: (1) 'Tolerance works while they are present' sits loosely beside the non-masking return, which is promised only once faults stop; 'Tolerance acts on faults that have arisen' would avoid the reading (the plan claim's 'returns to them, while faults are present' carries the same looseness). (2) 'its failure alone can defeat the claim' sits uneasily beside 'do not falsify the claim'; 'can defeat the properties the claim covers' is exact. (3) The cost sentence's last two clauses restate the paragraph's own fail-safe and non-masking sentences; only the masking-cost clause is new.
